aggregateCaveats: Equal-weight benchmark mix, not estimated production query frequency.

ABBA schedule separately rotates original/batch at1 and4 readers; two repeated runs per variant/reader, two warm rounds per run. Four samples/case is a small experiment and does not establish statistical significance or p95.
Process CPU uses100Hz user+system ticks, so individual CPU observations are quantized to10ms. Aggregated small differences can reflect quantization and runtime/GC variance.
Candidate phase timings are maximum shard elapsed time, not process CPU. Four-reader numeric-phase increase may reflect runtime/GC variance; no numeric code changed.
Do not extrapolate the isolated micro90% reduction to complete queries. Actual2M with catalog remains unmeasured for this proposal.

interpretation: Microbenchmark shows a large isolated guard-batching win:61% wall reduction at1worker and89–92% at4/8/12 for fixed total work. Process CPU similarly drops.

Real candidate phases improve on broad queries, but end-to-end4-reader gains are small and mixed. Four-reader archive import unfiltered57.575→58.334ms (+1.3%), email57.010→51.085ms (-10.4%); archive export54.949→53.404ms (-2.8%).
One-reader archive import115.313→112.699ms (-2.3%), archive export104.907→95.353ms (-9.1%); search56.195→44.691ms (-20.5%).
The100k corpus and engine-only memory proof do not establish2M latency or memory with the retained catalog. No claim of achieving500ms at2M.
All real-query physical read counters were0; this is warm CPU/SQLite evidence, not cold-device latency.
No SQL window enlargement, index-format changes, numeric-cache batching, score cutoffs, retained-key-readability state, or auth-error fallback introduced.
